utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1445, is it true that precisely on the same day when the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed that fierce fighting broke out in Sarajevo and other places and that 14 people were killed and over 100 wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 3rd of May a column of the JNA was attacked which was pulling out of the army command building in the centre of town that had been taken control of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I wasn't in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard about the event.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that these same groups of the Patriotic League, that they attacked the military convoy in Tuzla on the 15th of May when 49 soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that either because I wasn't in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, then; do you know anything about the arming of your forces from that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were a very respected functionary. I assume you know that already in October 1991, almost six months prior to the beginning of the armed struggle, that from Austria by plane to Sarajevo, a large quantity of weapons were flown in.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Here is the witness from Doboj, and you are making these generalised points through him. He said he wasn't in Sarajevo, and now we're going to go on to try these very general points about Austria and Sarajevo. I don't know what you think the purpose of cross-examination is but it appears that you think it is to put as much detail as you can about the Serb side, and I speak generally. Now, we've been going on this case for nearly two years, and you must understand that witnesses can only answer on matters of which they have direct knowledge. There is no point arguing with the witness or wasting time asking the witness about things about which he knows absolutely nothing. You, as I have said many, many times, can call your evidence on planes from Austria and the like. If it's relevant, you can call it, but there's no point wasting time with the witness on it. Now, just asking him something he can actually answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I cannot know in advance whether the witness knows something or not. That's why I'm asking him. And it is up to him to say that he really doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we waste time with generalised questions. He's already answered two questions. He wasn't in Tuzla; he wasn't in Sarajevo. Shall we see if he knows anything about planes from Austria and Sarajevo? Do you know anything about that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume I can ask him questions about Bosnia-Herzegovina, because he was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They don't have to be concrete ones like planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But anyway, do you know that already in January 1992, in Geneva, that the principles of the constitutional set-up were adopted which were proposed by the international intermediaries -- mediators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's come from Doboj. You can ask him about Doboj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this witness ought to know how the conflict came about. The conflicts did not break out because of Doboj but because of the overall situation that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask witnesses -- you've got witnesses coming who can deal with the general position. This gentleman is dealing with a particular municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1445, you said yourself that in the municipality, you functioned quite all right and that the representatives of the Serbs and Muslims and Croats cooperated right up until the divergence of ways with respect to the referendum and the issues posed there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did cooperate until the first parliamentary elections, because we had a common goal, to overthrow the Communist Party or, rather, the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you assumed power, then you quarrelled amongst yourselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't quarrel among ourselves. We went our separate ways because of ideology of the SDS party, because right after the takeover of power in Doboj, the SDS immediately, logically with acquiescence from its republican mentors, started along a separatist road which was not in conformity and in agreement with the other ethnic groups and parties in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these republican mentors of theirs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was common knowledge. A higher organ, the republican SDS led by Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you had a republican SDA party led by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think we can compare the role of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic with the role of Mr. Radovan Karadzic. Alija Izetbegovic is today a respected individual, which is visited by many international individuals and representatives from various countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Alija Izetbegovic, and that's another matter, but do you know that Alija Izetbegovic, once the agreement was signed at the beginning of 1992 on the part of three national parties, Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Boban, withdrew his signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that because I wasn't a high-ranking functionary either of the SDA or of state organs. I was just a republican deputy and one of the functionaries of the Doboj municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in paragraph 10 you say that the strategy of the SDS consisted of two phases and that before the elections in 1990, they propagated propaganda, as you said, as a democratic party and after the elections that they started a different kind of propaganda for a Greater Serbia and used legends to win over the population and its sympathies, and they organised this in every meeting and every village and regularly held meetings. When did you ever hear that somebody mentioned any kind of Greater Serbian goal? When did you hear about that and how can you say that in your statement in point 10?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's nothing that is -- wasn't known. Even the pre-electoral meetings in Doboj, Nikola Koljevic, one of the speakers and Radovan Karadzic and others, not in the sense of saying that this is going to be a Greater Serbia. They didn't actually say that, but we said that we must have the Serb people living in one state. So if it is one state, that means the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina populated by Serbs and that that -- they will be living in Serbia afterwards, that that would be Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia exist at the time? Was it one state, one country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was everybody living in one country, the Serbs and the Muslims Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. alike? There are many Muslims in Serbia, for instance. They all lived in one country, one state, and that state was Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question, and I don't think we ought to go back to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you hear that any of them mentioned -- you mentioned the meeting in Doboj. Did you hear anybody mention some kind of Greater Serbia at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a question of Greater Serbia but from the context of their speeches, that's what we concluded. And if we say that every Serb and all Serbs must live in one state, one country, then it is logical to deduce that the territory where they are living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the Serbs live in Bosnia-Herzegovina means that they will live in one state, whether it is Yugoslavia or whether you call it a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the future. I was talking about a reality where everybody was living in one country, one state in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's your opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's only my opinion, is it, that everybody lived in Yugoslavia, the Serbs and Muslims and Croats and Macedonians and Slovenes and Montenegrins. That's my opinion, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This sounds like an argument, which we're not going to get much further with. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this then: At those elections in 1990, who had the largest number of deputies in the Municipal Assembly of Doboj, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action -- no, the SDS party, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Serbs in your municipality won the largest number of votes, had the greatest number of deputies, and yet nonetheless, for the president of the municipality, a Muslim was elected to the post. The post was offered to a Muslim and the Muslim became the municipality president.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but along with a comment, if I may. The Party of Democratic Action was the second party. That is to say, it got 27 deputy seats -- seats in the Assembly, but the SDP and the reformist forces, both of them together as party, a democratic party, got a total of 26 seats. And knowing that the majority of Muslims, that is, over 90 per cent voted for those two parties, we did not want, because we used the Republican laws of the day, the electoral laws of the day, we did not want to set up a government within the space of two months; and pursuant to that law, unless you establish a government within the space of two months, the elections are repeated. And when we proposed this to the SDS, to have a new round of elections, the SDS straight away agreed to give the post of president to a member of the Democratic Action Party although it had a different position in the electoral results. Came second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that the SDS offered a Muslim to occupy the role of president of the municipality, you in fact forced them to do so. Is that what you're saying? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't force them to do that. We just used positive legal provisions because we quite certainly, in a repeated election, we would have had 10 per cent more votes than the SDS would have had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're not going to go into conjecture and surmise as to what would happen at elections that never took place. But tell me this, please: Immediately prior to these events in Doboj, is it true that in the territory north of Doboj regular units from neighbouring Croatia had entered as well as paramilitary formations that developed in the municipality and the town itself, but from the territories of neighbouring municipalities, Gracanica, Maglaj, Zavidovici, Zepa, and that they were engaged actively against Doboj? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. I never received any such report and I probably would have because the chief of the security centre was a member of the SDS of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me when these Muslim units were formed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Muslim formations or units up until the attack on Doboj. These formations were spontaneously formed, that is, units to defend the territory, when we had fled from Doboj towards Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the word "fled" from Doboj. In May 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when was the Patriotic League formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Patriotic League did not exist at all in Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will show you a document of yours. I don't mean you personally but of the Muslim side. The command of the 2nd Corps, strictly confidential, 28th of November, 1992. The information has to do with an incident, but one can see from it where the incident had occurred or, rather, what had prompted it. It says: "On the 27th of November, 1992, at 1600 hours, at the Tuzla hotel in Tuzla, the first anniversary was observed of the Patriotic League of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That is in November 1992, the first anniversary is being celebrated of the Patriotic League, which means that you formed in November 1991. How many months is that prior to the outbreak of the conflict? So months before the beginning of the conflict you have the Patriotic League and an organised army in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask those people from Tuzla, because I was never a member of the Patriotic League nor did it exist at all in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the commander of the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question? Which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he commander of the Main Staff at the very beginning and in the period that you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here his directive, dated the 25th of February, 1992. So long before that. After that comes March, April, and then May. So it means three months prior to any conflicts in Doboj. And he says: "Our forces are organised into the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina in units ranging from a platoon to detachments and brigades numbering a total of 120.000 men." And he writes this in a directive dated the 25th of February. There were no conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then he says: "The beginning of combat operations will lead to greater numbers of members of the MUP and the Yugoslav army and Muslim people outside the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina joining so that the effective strength will be about 150.000 men." He talks about detachments and brigades as a reality already in February 1992. The Patriotic League was founded in 1991. Surely you -- it is not possible that you don't know anything about that, Mr. 1445.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, sir. You will ask Mr. Sefer Halilovic. I was never a member of any command and I was not aware of these things nor did it interest me. I was concerned with the citizens of Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, could this be admitted into evidence, this document of the command of the 2nd Corps referring to the first anniversary of the Patriotic League? It speaks of an incident that occurred at that event, but it is clear that the incident occurred during the celebrations of the first anniversary of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the document first and then we'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, just look at the first sentence. The incident itself is of no interest to me. This happened among your own participants at the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would look at it, confirm that it says what the accused says it says. And if you have any comment, of course you can make it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment to make. I see Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this for the first time, and I hear it for the first time of any kind of incident or this meeting and this anniversary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us see it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification. Give it the next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D195 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since I have very little time, I will show you a few more documents. Some are from the army of Republika Srpska, and some from the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the opposing side. And I will only show you those in which Doboj is mentioned. For instance, this is a report on offensive operations from the 13th to the 19th of January, 1993, an infantry attack was carried out in the area around Gradacac and Doboj and on the town of Doboj itself. Fire was opened from 120-millimetre mortars from the region of Bukova. I assume you know this because you were firing at Doboj. Then another one, 15th of January. Fire was opened on a broader area of Doboj and Gradacac. Are you aware of these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of them. I would like to intervene. I would like to ask Mr. Milosevic not to claim that I know these things, because if he wants to ask me something, then he should ask me rather than saying that I know these things. I don't know them. I was not a soldier, and I certainly was not involved in any combat, and nobody sent me reports about battles around Doboj. You should ask other people about that who are relevant for these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. B-1445, you must bear with the accused. We have only a limited number of witnesses, as you know, here because of the constraints of time. It so happens that you have come here to speak of Doboj and, therefore, he's entitled to put matters about Doboj to you. If you don't know the answer, of course just say so, but it may be that there are other witnesses who could speak to these matters. Do you want this exhibit produced, Mr. Milosevic, this report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to quote from several of them, and then I will offer all of them together and you will decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You must do them one at a time, because otherwise the thing will become disordered. Let the witness see this first document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the passages highlighted. One can see from the report that there was action against Doboj. Then on the 9th of January as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, wait a moment. One at a time. Just let the witness have a look, and if he's got any comment, to make it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, we can't see who is sending it nor which institution is involved. He mentions a military unit, but I can't see it. There's nothing in the heading, just offensive activities of Muslim forces in such-and-such a period. I can't comment on it, nor do I know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about those events in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know? I wasn't living in Doboj at the time. I was chased out of Doboj and was living in a neighbouring town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A neighbouring town from which fire was opened on Doboj. That was the line from which fire was opened at Doboj. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, when we fled over there and formed a Crisis Staff and a TO staff, those were military units, and logically there was an exchange of fire. But you should ask them, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you an official at the time when this was happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to deal with this -- we're going to deal with this document first if you want it exhibited. Let us see it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give it the next exhibit number, but we will only mark it for identification having heard what the witness says about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D196, Your Honour, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the Prosecution, of course, can see these documents as they are produced. Yes. Do you want to produce another one, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, since the witness has commented that these Serb reports do not have an indication of who is sending them, I will give him Muslim reports on which one can see who is sending them, where they are coming from. For instance, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Supreme Command Staff, strictly confidential, 02428/1, to the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state on the battlefields of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I will quote only from paragraph 4 because Doboj is mentioned. "The free territory of Doboj and Tesanj was yesterday fiercely attacked with armoured mechanised units, artillery and helicopter units." And then it says: "Our forces responded readily and inflicted heavy losses on the aggressor, destroyed seven tanks and three OTDs." So that is paragraph 4 alone. And the signatory is Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic. So your units, and in this report which he's sending to Izetbegovic, who is attending talks somewhere, says that they destroyed seven tanks and three -- what he calls OTDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date of this report, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 22nd of March, 1993. There was a war going on over there all the time, from the spring 1992 until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see this document if you want to produce it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has not been confirmed or signed. Anyone could have written it. You can see for yourself. And I comment -- I cannot comment on it. Even if it were authentic, then it is a document of the Commander-in-Chief of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't asked you whether the document was addressed to you. I am asking you in connection with the events that your commander calls the Doboj theatre of war. Are you familiar with those events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am familiar with many events, but I don't know the dates because the free territory of Doboj municipality was attacked throughout the two-and-a-half-year period, from the 5th of May when an aggression on Doboj was carried out. Our fighters over there defended that whole area, and there were thousands of such attacks by Serb units. All I -- all -- the only people that can confirm it are the military commanders and people who were in the military. I was in the civilian organs of authority of Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us -- let us see the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the date and the number, and everything a document needs to have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without a signature or a stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will mark that for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D197 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next document, Report on Combat Activities, it says: "Operative Group 7 Doboj, state of ammunition is alarming," which indicates that you had used up a great deal of ammunition firing at Serb positions. Is it true that throughout the period from May 1992 until 1995 there was an uninterrupted battle around Doboj? Fighting was going on between the two sides. Isn't that beyond doubt, Mr. 1445?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting continued, but the attacks were coming from the Serb Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. side. Throughout the period, as I said a moment ago, from the 5th of May 1992 until the signing of the Dayton Accords, Serb forces were constantly attacking the free territory of Doboj municipality. And I have to make a comment. You need to know that the international community enforced an embargo on weapons. And if the gentleman says that we fired the ammunition, you didn't -- we didn't have ammunition or weapons, and you provided the logistics for the Serb forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you manage to destroy tanks and three armoured APCs and to kill so many people? You probably did that without ammunition or weapons, or using hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how we obtained ammunition, but certainly there was some way of getting it. As far as I know, in those days there were two elements of the army. The HVO was there, too, and they probably provided some aid and ammunition, but I'm unable to comment on these things because I wasn't a military commander, nor was I a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you remember that Izetbegovic himself said, "We have managed to procure 300.000 rifles and machine-guns, 20 million ammunition, 37.000 mines, 46.000 shells"? This was his own statement when he was talking about the weapons that had been procured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your statement. I never heard of any such statement by Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It will be easy to confirm it. As you say that you were the ones who were attacked, we have here a protest letter by the Serb side, and it was written and signed and probably exists in the archives of UNPROFOR, to the command of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak to Mr. -- or, rather, General Nambiar personally, a protest it says, and then the document was signed by the Chief of Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, Major General Manojlo Milovanovic. Somebody signed for him but it does have a stamp. And it states: "At the very outset in the border area of Gradacac, Doboj and Teslic, the artillery opened fire from the region of Pojica, Tulovici, Debelo Brdo, Matuzici and Alibegovici, and from the region of Demilic Planja there was fire against armoured missiles." So do you know about these events, events for which the Serb side is protesting -- is lodging a protest with the commander of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 17th of January, 1993. You can take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the 18th of January, as well, the next letter. Then the 19th of January, another one. So each of those letters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, one at a time. We'll deal with these one at a time. We'll begin with the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you are. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have taken a look at this document. However, how can I be asked to comment about a protest to the commander of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak, Mr. Nambiar, whereas I was living in Tesanj and working in the civilian organs of power and authority? You don't assume that Nambiar came to inform me about events of this kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Produce -- don't interrupt. Produce the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter is addressed to the commander of UNPROFOR, but what I am saying relates to Doboj. It also relates to other matters as well, and I have marked the sections relating to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification. It will get the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 198 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What are the -- what are the next exhibits you have? The witness doesn't want to look at them, waste of time. Give them to us. Yes, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have the 18th of January, the 19th of January, also documents signed in the same way, and they refer to continuous action against Doboj and Teslic from the artillery and infantry weapons attacking Serb settlements. And then in the next document, it goes on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just stop there. The 18th and the 19th, are they similar protests to the one of the 17th or are they different sorts of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're the same sorts of documents, and they're all addressed to General Nambiar. They're all signed. When we're talking about sorts of documents, by the Chief of Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, but they do differ on some points, because here this document speaks of artillery attacks on Serb settlements and artillery and infantry attacks, and then in the next document it refers to Doboj, Teslic and Gradacac, attacks by Muslim forces and then in the following one, once again Doboj, Maslacik [phoen], and Teslic, and other places too. But these are all letters of protest that were sent to General Nambiar, and he was on the spot and was able to check this out and see for himself. So this probably or most certainly this exists in the UNPROFOR archives and you can take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just -- just -- before the usher brings them, let us make sure we have for the record what it is you're putting in. We've got the 17th already. That is the -- I think that's got a number. Just one moment. I think what we might do is put them all together in one exhibit. So we've got the 17th, the 18th, and the 19th. Is that right, Mr. Milosevic? 17th, 18th and 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll add these further documents to the -- whatever the last number was. 198. So they will form one bundle of protests. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to hurry up here. We have a report here referring to units of regular armed forces of the Republic of Croatia which are engaged in combat activities against the army of Republika Srpska on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then we can see July 1992 in the region of Bosanski Brod. And then further on, I don't have time to go through all of this, I'm just going to read out an observation, the concluding observation, and it lists the dates and mentions the names of the units in the area of Republika Srpska on its territory. There are continuous engagements of 15 brigades, regular armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, the equivalent of about 30.000 men, about 270 artillery pieces are used, over 76-millimetre calibre. The ones up to 76-millilitres are not considered to be vital and about 75 armoured vehicles, tanks and transporters, APCs. So that is what this piece of information contains. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The connection to Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is in the northerly part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. 1445, about this period of time and anything about the presence of regular Croatian forces in that territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I myself was in quite the opposite area, in the south. I wasn't in the north, as you just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was all over the region. Fifteen brigades, 30.000 men. They weren't deployed in one spot. You have a whole area. Bosanski Brod, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for example, is fairly close by, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that from the 5th of March, we went to the southern side towards Tesanj. So I wasn't able to receive any information about any number of soldiers or units either with regard to Brod, Derventa or Modrica because in actual fact, it was in quite another section. So we were completely cut off communication-wise. Between us were the forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many kilometres is it from the broader region around Bosanski Brod to the place where you were at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 85 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was -- there were great operations there and concentration of forces and you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never lived there. I was never down there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you going to take these documents, Mr. May? They speak about very large numbers of men and units on the territory of Republika Srpska, and it mentions the number of the -- the numbers of the brigades, their composition, their origin, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is the -- who is the report from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report is by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, pass it -- pass it up. Let us have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You won't ask anything for the moment until we have just finished this, look at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We notice it's not signed or stamped or has anything to indicate what it might be, but we'll mark it for identification. We'll give it the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D199, Your Honour, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a report, not information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go -- we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we do if we're going to talk about this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about the creation of the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And saying that most of them had previously been in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to your army, were also most of the members previously in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the period prior to the 5th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1445, a moment ago we established, and this can be seen from the documents and those need to prove it, you know it yourself, Sefer Halilovic was commander of the Main Staff. Before that, he was a JNA officer. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was the first commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was after the 5th of May or, rather, the 3rd of May, 1992. So you have to distinguish between these two things. We're talking about the attack on Doboj, events prior to that, and events after it. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that Sefer Halilovic was not the commander prior to the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this directive that I have and that was published even in his book, a photocopy of it, is dated the 25th of February, 1992, and he says there that -- how the forces were organised, that is, 120.000 men, the Patriotic League, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was the first Chief of Staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not formed before the 3rd of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't wish to argue with you, because the documents contain dates far before the 3rd of May, 1992. But I asked you whether Sefer Halilovic had come from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic fled from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Sefer Halilovic from Bosnia and Herzegovina perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic is a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, but he's from Serbia. He never even served in Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, whether he came from Serbia -- he's originally from Sandzak. Whether in those days he was a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not argue about this particular point. No doubt it can be cleared up. Mr. Milosevic, you have one minute left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said an hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we started at several minutes after 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right. You're right. You've got another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Then I'll cover the new documents quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just make sure about one thing. The commander of the Main Staff, Sefer Halilovic, is from Serbia, from Prijepolje. He was defending Bosnia from an aggressor, the commander of which is Ratko Mladic from Kalinovik from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Doesn't that seem absurd to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are all general points. They aren't matters for the witness at all. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just cover these exhibits which I received the day before yesterday and not on the 13th as stated. Please look at the additional statement of the witness, paragraph 5. You say: "I do not recognise the signature at the bottom of the document as being Milan Ninkovic's. I knew Milan Ninkovic personally." How then can this document be exhibited through you? Then on the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. Let the witness have the document. Which is the tab?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 1, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that's Prosecution Exhibit 562.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is it you want the witness to look at? Paragraph 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. He says, the witness says and I quote him: "I do not recognise the signature at the bottom of the document as being Milan Ninkovic's signature." Yet he's identifying the document alleged by signed by Ninkovic. So I'm just giving an example of the way in which exhibits are being introduced and produced. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, wait a moment. Let the witness answer that. And presumably we're talking, are we, about the documents at tab 4, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we don't have time for all this, Mr. May. You will interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only thing is that the witness must have a chance to comment, you see, when you make a point. Yes. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signature is here where it says for, so it's not Ninkovic who signed it but somebody else for him, his secretary or somebody else. So in the document itself you see the word "za," "for," which means that the signature is not of Milan Ninkovic but somebody else's. It is written in the document. So I don't see anything at issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in -- we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this additional statement of yours, you claim that you recognised the voices of Momcilo Krajisnik and Radovan Karadzic because you knew them. And then you say: "As regards Mr. Karadzic, I recognised his accent though the sound in this conversation differs from the tone of voice he used in the Assembly."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He speaks differently, yet you recognise him. How is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I listened to Mr. Karadzic several times as a member of parliament. His accent can be recognised by anyone who hears him for once. However, in this conversation with his close associate, he spoke so quietly, and it was -- that is why I said there was a difference, whereas when he speaks at the rostrum in the Assembly, he's arrogant, he threatens, he hurls insults, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume those speeches in the Assembly were broadcast by television and reported in the press. I don't remember him insulting anyone in those speeches of his, at least the ones that we had access to in Serbia from your news programmes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is not insulting for you when he, as president of the SDS, says in the Assembly that a whole nation will disappear if we don't agree to live in Yugoslavia, then I don't know what an insult is in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know of that statement of his, just as you don't know about Izetbegovic's that were published in the press. But let's look at some other tabs. There are various local communities, in most cases villages, aren't they? A village constitutes a local commune. Isn't that right, Mr. 1445?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now people are spontaneously making decisions, and it says: "With a view to fulfilling the freely expressed wish of the Serb people to live within the SFRY as a community of free and equal peoples ..." As a community of free and equal peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I note this for the record; it's tab 2. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. 1445, because you speak of certain other characteristics. Now, these people who are making decisions, virtually expressing loyalty to the state in which they were living and in which they had lived for all of 70 years, ever since Yugoslavia was formed, and they describe Yugoslavia as a community of free and equal peoples. They talk about the equality of peoples and loyalty to their country, and as you are tendering this as an exhibit, this appears to be a crime to be loyal to one's one country, to one's own nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That isn't a matter for the witness. This is a pure comment. Now you have now one minute left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't have time to cover these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why in your examination-in-chief you explained that you saw Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Karadzic at a rally and at a secret meeting? There was no secret meeting. Under tab 5, it says, an announcement: On the 5th of February, 1992 at 12.00 at Doboj in the premises of the business bank - a public institution - a meeting will be held of presidents of municipal boards of the SDS of Bosnian Krajina and will be attended by Dr. Radovan Karadzic as president of the party. Why are you describing it as a secret meeting when, in addition, we have the newspaper which published the debate at that meeting? Why did you describe that meeting in that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This announcement was addressed to municipal boards of the Serbian Democratic Party, and that meeting was completely closed to the public. It was only after the meeting that reports appear in the press for the public. So at that point in time, it was a completely closed meeting, and it was heavily secured. No one could go in or come out except the people invited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've had your time now. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack, have you any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour Re-examined by Ms. Pack:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just referring back to -- if we could go into private session very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1445, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. If you would just wait one minute while the blinds are brought down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's close to the time for the next break, so we'll adjourn before we take the next break -- the next witness, but it may be convenient to deal with the administrative matter which I mentioned yesterday, which is in relation to Lord Owen, the length of examination which the parties would ask for. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would request a period of two hours with which to examine Lord Owen and would request that that period be bifurcated so the Prosecution had 15 minutes to question him after the accused questioned him. And the Prosecution would not be opposing each of the parties have some period of time in reserve so that we can clear up matters raised by the accused or the amici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you want cross-examination and then a re-cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be an opportunity to ask questions. Mr. Nice has asked if he could address you on this personally. It arises from his experience in the Kordic case and wanted to address the Chamber upon his return next week, but that is -- will be his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That it be bifurcated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll think about that. We need to make an order soon, that's the problem, but we'll consider it. Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Nice -- Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dealing first of all with the Prosecution request, in our submission it wouldn't be appropriate for the Prosecution to have a second bite of the cherry and after the other parties have questioned the witness for them to then seek to put matters their way after the previous questioning. This is a witness who is to be examined in front of the Trial Chamber by all parties on equal terms. We all come to the Tribunal, as it's written in the Statute, with an equality. To give the Prosecution extra advantage, in our submission, would not be right, bearing in mind to a great extent the reason why we're having this witness has been through their own endeavours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what if you were also given a second bite?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then Mr. Nice would want a third bite, because they never sit down, Your Honour, and that's been the history. I know Your Honour has mentioned this several times during applications, saying, "Don't you take no for an answer?" And we could go on and on. It might be better if everyone just has their period and -- and are -- use their efforts within that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have any time you want to put forward yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It would not be more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, unfortunately because of the enormous number of documents and the material that I receive, I haven't had time to look at what has been served on me for Lord Owen's testimony, so I have no proper idea about it. But I judge that one day would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll think about this and we'll draft an appropriate order. We'll adjourn now and sit again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Witness Sead Omeragic, and there are no protective measures for this witness. He will be given by traditional 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha. Examined by Mr. Agha:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you give a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecution in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequently in July of this year, did you certify that statement before the Registry of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that statement before you and signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I kindly ask the Court to allow an exhibit number to be allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 563, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that includes -- you're perhaps going to come on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to deal with the article. That includes the article itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The article itself isn't actually attached to the bis but I would hope to present that separately and have a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. You're asking us to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will a separate exhibit number for the article.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 564, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, since this is a 92 bis witness, I will just read in essence a brief summary of the witness's testimony and then, if I may with your permission, ask a few viva voce questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, the witness has worked as a journalist since 1983. On the 4th of April, 1992, the witness travelled from Sarajevo to Bijeljina with Fikret Abdic and two others. On the 4th of April, the witness wrote an article which was published in Slobodna Bosna on the 10th of April, which has just been exhibited. The witness stands by this article except for the reference in it to Mauzer, which was a case of mistaken identity, and the reference to him drinking Raki for two hours. They drove by road in a convoy and were accompanied by Biljana Plavsic and General Prascevic, whose vehicles were behind them. On the way to Bijeljina, they passed Serb, Croatian, and Bosniak roadblocks. As the convoy entered Bijeljina, the witness saw two mosques, both of which were flying Serbian flags. He also heard Radio Bijeljina announce that 25 bodies had been found in a garbage dump. The witness became scared and announced that these were Bosniak bodies. On arrival, they went to the JNA barracks where they found about 300 to 400 men, women, and children taking shelter. These people were crying and surrounded Abdic, thinking that he would save them. The people told him that they were not killers and were not to blame for anything. Plavsic was present, standing about 50 metres away. The witness then accompanied Abdic, Plavsic, and General Prascevic to the municipal building, where they met with Arkan. The witness was standing next to General Prascevic when Prascevic met Arkan, and the witness formed the impression that Arkan was in fact Prascevic's main commander. Plavsic was next to General Prascevic when he reported to Arkan, and the witness saw Plavsic embrace and kiss Arkan. The Generals Prascevic and Jankovic, who were both present, showed great respect for Plavsic who appeared to have political power over them. In front of Abdic and Arkan, Plavsic said that Arkan had saved Bijeljina from the crimes which the Muslims had prepared against the Serbs. The witness was told by a member of the TO that they had killed "quite a lot of balijas." The witness saw Goran Hadzic arrive and go into the municipal building and join the meeting with Arkan, Plavsic, and Abdic. He was not allowed to attend the meeting. Abdic was the only Muslim that attended. B-1489, a Serbian journalist, was invited to attend. There were two men with a camera from Sarajevo TV who Arkan had not allowed to attend the meeting. One of Arkan's men with four others in green uniforms removed the two men when they found that they were from Sarajevo TV, declaring that it was "Alija's TV." The witness also saw another man being ordered by one of Arkan's men to be taken away when he was unable to produce his documents. The witness then heard a shot. Arkan's man then took out his pistol and pointed it at the witness's head and told Prascevic's aid not to make him kill the witness in front of his eyes. Arkan, however, came out of the meeting and made a gesture with his finger to go away. Everyone left. The men with the old JNA uniforms were obeying Arkan's man, and finally, the order of Arkan. The witness then went on a tour of the town with Plavsic and Arkan. The witness observed that the people in Bijeljina were very distressed. Abdic made a speech to placate the Muslims, which Abdic thought was being broadcast over the radio --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. -- but music was being played instead. Outside the municipal hall, the witness heard Arkan say that he was going to Bosanski Brod to deal with "that mother Armin Pohara" who at that time was leader of the Croat and Bosniak resistance in Bosanski Brod. Plavsic was close by and would have heard Arkan say this. A woman approached the witness and told Abdic that they had killed 22 people in a basement and that they had tortured and killed a boxer and that they had committed atrocities and it was a tragedy. Abdic simply walked away. The witness then left Bijeljina and went to Tuzla JNA headquarters where he attended a meeting in the officers' dining-room. In the meeting were Plavsic, Abdic, General Jankovic, Colonel Dubajic, General Prascevic, and a couple of other lower-ranking JNA officers. At the meeting, Plavsic declared that Arkan had saved Bijeljina from crimes against the Serbs which the Muslims had prepared for Bajram. The witness got into an argument with Plavsic and asked how could she say such a thing. She had seen the situation in Bijeljina where the Muslims had fled to the barracks and had even been told that 27 Muslims had been killed there. The witness told Plavsic that he was not happy with the way she was dealing with things and that she was lying in front of the officers. Plavsic told him that more Serbs had been killed and that Serbs were always the ones in danger of attack. At the meeting, the witness told Colonel Dubajic and the other officers present that if they had an officer's honour, they would say that atrocities were committed against Muslims in Bijeljina. Everyone then became quiet, and the witness realised that he was in a dangerous position. The witness looked at General Jankovic who had a terrified, astonished look in his eyes. After awhile, General Jankovic covered his heads with his hands and admitted that many, many more Muslims had been killed in Bijeljina than Serbs. Now, this is the essence of the witness's statement, and with the permission of the Court, I would like him just briefly to comment upon two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first exhibit is the one which was of the article and given the exhibit number by Your Honours. Can we kindly show the witness a copy of this article? It's Exhibit 564. Witness, can you please tell the Chamber whether you wrote this article and it is the basis of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This article is the basis for my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, may I also briefly show a video clip to the witness which has previously been tendered in Exhibit 425 as tab number 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And I would just kindly ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would please look at your screen and have a quick look at the video clip and tell us the people in the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. I can see on the left Mr. Andric, General Prascevic, and at the end myself, the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Would you please continue the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the witness tell us what he observed personally?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I observed at this point Arkan and Mrs. Plavsic, and that's when, as you can see, they kissed. I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if I may with the Court's permission, just ask a couple of viva voce questions to the witness which came out of his proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the time when you went to Bijeljina with General Prascevic and General Jankovic, what positions of seniority were they holding at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Prascevic, I assume, was the deputy in the 2nd Army District of the commander General Kukanjac. And General Jankovic was the commander of the Tuzla Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, they were very senior positions of authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were extremely senior positions in the army, in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your statement that you also met a journalist by the name of Mrkic. Can you kindly tell the Chamber if any clearing-up operations were carried out prior to Mrs. Plavsic's visit?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In talking to people that I met with the soldiers, ordinary people, I would learn various things by the way, including the fact that before that, there were conflicts and that there were tens of people dead, that everything took place out in the streets, and the streets -- that the streets were later cleared of the blood from the corpses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the corpses also removed prior to the visit?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I learnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you say in your statement you went to the JNA barracks. Did General Jankovic tell you whether any other Muslims were detained anywhere else, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: General Jankovic addressed Fikret Abdic and told him that in addition to those several hundred refugees who were there in the barracks where we were, there were another one an a half thousand refugees, mostly Muslims, in Petkovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you were with Mrs. Plavsic, was there ever a suggestion that the JNA should take over control of the town from Arkan and the paramilitaries, and if there was, can you tell us who made the suggestion and what the response was, please?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Precisely on the footage that we just saw when General Prascevic is reporting in front of Arkan, that's when some strange things happened. I would -- I thought this was quite strange requests, that Arkan should leave the town to the Yugoslav People's Army, and he expressly refused to do so, and as you said, he added that he would go to Bosanski Brod and settle accounts there, and he swore with the army there, with Armin Pohara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for cutting you off, Witness. Now, when Arkan expressly refused to hand over control to the JNA, did he explain why?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not the army there but with Armin Pohara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, he said that he had to deal with the situation in Bijeljina, and only afterwards to go on to Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you understand him to mean by dealing with the situation in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: First of all, I asked myself how was it possible that the army who was powerful and yet -- and a general is entreating and asking for something, a man who had several hundred people behind him, asked to hand over the town. And second, I thought he had to deal with -- well, I couldn't understand what this was about, what was supposed to be done to deal with the situation in the town, perhaps to settle affairs politically speaking, or I don't know how, to set things in order there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Witness, can you tell us if you learnt anything about what was happening to any of the mosques in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: At the time, I saw two flags, we can call them Serbian flags, up on two mosques in Bijeljina. While we were driving through the town and moving towards the barracks, I said, "Look at that, Mr. Abdic. They've hung up the flags." And some ten metres later, he said, "No, they haven't hung up any flags. What are you talking about?" The driver stopped, the driver driving us all stopped. Suddenly he had to slam down the breaks, and he said, "Mr. President, take a look. You can see two flags there. Yes, they have." And I had become accustomed to Mr. Abdic's reactions of this kind. I think he was afraid. And at that point in time, he was being filmed by some secret services so he was under that impression and was afraid probably. And rumour had it - I learnt this by talking to people, how it came about - that some of the mosques were looted. That's what I heard, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That would conclude the examination-in-chief. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one thing to clear up. Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Omeragic, you were a journalist of Slobodna Bosna, the Fokus, Dnevni Avaz, Oslobodjenje, and Vecernje Novosti, all those papers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I worked less for Oslobodjenje and Vecernje Novosti, on very few occasions, and I state that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you're a war reporter from Slobodna Bosna and the Liljan paper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you collaborated with other papers, I assume you sent out some of your articles to them from time to time. Did that date back to the war in Bosnia, during that time or before that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Somewhere from 1992 up until the 15th of January, 1993, I worked for the paper Slobodna Bosna. After that, several journalists left Sarajevo, which was under siege, for us to be able to report from parts of Bosnia that were under the control of the army, not to stay in Sarajevo only. So after that, some of us were engaged by the Liljan paper. That was the only paper that was printed because there was no paper to print the news on except for the paper Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, with Fikret Abdic, you came to Bijeljina, and as far as my information tells me, that was on the 6th of April, and you reported on the events that took place on the 4th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I can't quite remember the date exactly, but I do know that I was in Bijeljina on the 4th of April. Now, as to the exact date, I really can't say when I made a note of this and reported this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have just heard in the explanations given that in your text you reported something that did not take place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a mistake, a mistaken identity, actually, referring to the man under the nickname of Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In your article, you say you met Ljubisa Savic, called Mauzer, but you did not in fact meet that particular man. And in paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that: "In the article I say I mentioned Ljubisa Savic, known as Mauzer. I later saw photos of Mauzer and realised that it wasn't Mauzer that I had met but one of Arkan's men."

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be allowed to explain? During my stay in the Bijeljina municipality building, I saw a man whom I was to recognise on photographs later on as being Mauzer. It was Ljubisa Savic, who at the time was wearing a JNA uniform, and I think that on the occasion, he had some sort of privileged position in the eyes of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. I remember that moment very well, and I can explain it to you. When, to a soldier wearing a JNA uniform, whether it was the Territorial Defence or something else, I don't know, or whether it was a regular army member, dropped his rifle, Arkan went up to the man, and I think he slapped him and said, "Pick up the rifle, and you're demobilised as of now." I experienced something similar in front of the municipality building. I remembered the face of that young man, and I was later to learn that he was Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. He kept playing with a knife, a two-edged, two-bladed JNA knife. The knife dropped out of his hands at one point, and as he saw the slapping of this soldier and the fact that he had been demobilised on the spot, he became afraid, and he went all red in the face. And I was standing next to him and noticed this face of his, what it looked like, and I could never forget that face ever afterwards because of this sudden fear that he showed on his face. And later on in some papers, I saw that this was indeed Ljubisa Savic. And the man whom I thought was Mauzer to begin with, that was in fact Arkan's man who was wearing a black uniform and who had the various insignia denoting the Tigers. So much by way of explanation from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're actually confirming that you wrote that you met Mauzer, and you have now explained that or, rather, 11 years later you said that it wasn't correct. Is that the only thing that is not correct in this article of yours?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to explain that in 1996 or 1997, I saw the photograph of Ljubisa Savic, who was said to be Mauzer, and it was then that I recognised him. So not 12 years later but three or four years later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, but I am talking about your article, and it was only in 2001, when you were making your statement, you said that this was not correct. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that that man that you met with was actually Arkan's man. How did you know that he was Arkan's man?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of his uniform and the Tiger patch, the head of a tiger with his jaws wide open. And they wore this on their left sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So it means that at the time you thought that Ljubisa Savic, who is from Bijeljina, and I assume you knew that, that he too was a member of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa Savic was wearing an olive-grey uniform of the JNA therefore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But when you wrote this article and mistook him for Arkan's man, you considered him to be an Arkan Tiger, because you later on established that he was wearing a Tiger uniform.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: This was just a mistaken identity. I think there's nothing questionable about it. I just thought that one person was somebody, after which I saw a photograph and realised that he wasn't that person but someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from Fikret Abdic and Biljana Plavsic -- did they travel together?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in different cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In different cars, but they came to Bijeljina together, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were in the car with Abdic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Plavsic's car was in the same column, I assume. There were several cars constituting that column.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Biljana Plavsic was in a car behind yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, when we were going from Sarajevo, but at times they would change. If there were assumed to be any barricades on the road or when we were passing through places with a majority Serb population or Bosniak or Croat population, they would change places; Fikret Abdic would be in the first car, in the front car, and Mrs. Plavsic in the second. Or if we were passing through areas that she might control, in a sense, then she would go up front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But - very well - there's no doubt, however, that you did come across obstacles, blockades, barricades, which, as you yourself describe, some were held by Serbs, some by Croats, and some by Bosniaks. That is what you said in your statement. So all the parties had some sort of blockades and barricades.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that as we were driving towards Bijeljina, there were some just soldiers that we saw, but the first obstacles we came across with piles of sandbags was in front of the entry to Bijeljina.
