And as we returned, there may have been some hedgehog-shaped obstacles on the way back, maybe in two places. Near Zenica, I think, and I don't remember that we came across any others. But they were along the road, they didn't cause any particular problem. The first major obstacle on the road was in the form of a yellow truck standing across the road and a large pile of sand and two smaller piles of gravel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you are telling us. I'm just referring to paragraph 4 in your statement when you say, "Roadblocks were erected on the road to Bijeljina manned sometimes by Serbs and sometimes by Croats and Bosniaks. What I'm saying is that there were obstacles manned by various parties; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: One could say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And then you say that the curtains were closed. There was no one. And then at times you would see somebody peeping at you from behind the curtains. You noticed that the eyes were full of fear. The events were the events of war, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain. At the very entrance to Bijeljina, while we were driving, we slowed down at a certain point, and along the whole trip, over a distance of some six or seven kilometres, every ten metres or so, on both sides of the road, there were soldiers wearing JNA uniforms, and they were looking away from the road, with their guns pointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're trying to tell us is that they were securing the road, because they had their backs turned to the road and they were looking at either side of the road.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that was probably the reason for the fear of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I understand it, two members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina are travelling, and most frequently in such cases there is security with their backs turned to the road along which the people they are securing are passing, and they are observing either side of the road. They were securing Fikret Abdic and Biljana Plavsic or, rather, all of you who were coming, but I assume that the security detail was there because of the two members of the Presidency. Isn't that normal?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, though at the same time my impression was that it was a kind of show of force, because after all, there were too many soldiers, every ten metres or so, on either side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The visit had been unannounced, I assume, and they thought because of the events and the disturbances, the violence, the killings, they felt it their duty to secure the route that would be taken by two members of the Presidency on arriving to Bijeljina; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I don't see this in your article, though I did read through it quickly, did you know what was going on before your arrival there? What was happening in Bijeljina before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No. We had no information. There were rumours that there were disorders. We saw footage showing Arkan's troops firing at a building, shooting at a building, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear, because as a reporter, I assume you inquired into all events, that on the 31st of March, from the Istanbul coffee bar fire was opened across the road to the Srbija coffee bar, and an incident occurred provoked by the Muslim side. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I was only visiting the wounded, the people wounded from that coffee bar who were in hospital. However, whatever question I asked or any step I took, I was accompanied by one of Arkan's men, so I couldn't really ask anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know that previously the Muslims had captured the town and were distributing weapons in the premises of the SDA, and it was Alija Saracevic who was distributing those weapons?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that they had set up sniper nests on the water tower and the Zitopromet silo?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you inform yourself as to how these events had taken place in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: You saw that I went to Bijeljina at the last moment, and I agreed to go to Bijeljina because I heard that there was a problem over there which I needed to explain, and I set off without any prior knowledge about these things that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: We have already reviewed the events in Bijeljina here, but as you yourself were not present when they occurred, I won't ask you about them. But tell me, when listening to Radio Bijeljina, you heard, as far as I can see, that 25 bodies were found. On what grounds did you come to the conclusion that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: First of all, I heard that. I have ears, and I heard very well that these were 25 bodies found at the rubbish dump.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not my question, as to what you heard. If they captured Bijeljina, they probably captured the radio station and all the major facilities. The point of my question is on what grounds did you come to the conclusion that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I already had some experience with things like that as I had been to some other theatres of war, and I know well that when I say that they were Muslims, I assumed well that they would be the victims. They weren't well-armed, and they were only just preparing for the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you assumed that they were Muslims or did you have any facts on the basis of which you could say that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you say that they didn't have weapons, what did they open fire with from the Istanbul coffee bar, and how did they manage to set up sniper nests on the water tower, silo, and at the barricades in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Milosevic. Somebody sets up a sniper nest or a barricade, there must be victims of those numerous snipers and barricades that were allegedly armed, but as far as I was able to see over there, Radio Bijeljina announced that there were 41 victims, of which two were Serbs and one an old Croat lady who was killed accidentally on her balcony. So I don't know what those snipers were doing. Maybe they were just watching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they had blocked the town, according to the information I have, but you say that you saw - and it says this in your article - you saw a coffin with an old lady, Mirjana Ilic, who had been killed by a stray bullet, and according to my information it was not a stray bullet but that she was killed and killed by the Muslims. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No. After subsequent inquiries, I was told that she would -- had been killed by a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So subsequent inquiries, yet you published this article straight away.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you learnt later that she had been killed by a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you; while we were in that family -- with that family and watching the body of that old lady, as far as I can remember, they said that she had been killed by a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you reported that on the basis of what you were told at the time.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You then went to the JNA barracks as a safe place; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the JNA barracks as a place which should have been safe, I assume.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abdic negotiated where he would go with Mrs. Plavsic, and I was a person who thought to join in as an escort, and we found ourselves in the barracks where the people had fled to to seek shelter, as I had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us specify. A moment ago, it was mentioned that there were, according to my notes - I may be mistaken - that there were about 300 people there, is that right, in the barracks? That's what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said a moment ago - you can check - I said there were several hundred people. It is impossible to tell the exact number, the more so if you find yourself in such a crowd of people and you can't review it or assess it. There were several hundred people who were in a panic, people who were speaking with fear, with -- under stress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I just wanted to make this point clear to establish the facts. You say in paragraph 9 of your statement there were about 700 or 800 people hiding in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they surrounded Fikret Abdic and said, "We're not killers. We're not to blame for anything," et cetera. There were men and women and small children and babies and old people.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Mostly women, elderly women, some younger women and children, and maybe an elderly man or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they mostly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: We couldn't really determine who was who, but I think it was a mixed group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it quite clear that those people came to the JNA barracks to seek shelter, to seek protection?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they given protection over there? Were they protected?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: They were over there. I can't say anything more than that, nor do I know anything else, but they did go there to seek shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you whether they were protected there, because we have heard claims here that the JNA was jeopardising those people. Could you establish any such thing when you went there? They went there because they felt safe and sought protection.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: If I may answer. If I may explain. Because Arkan and his units was attacking Bijeljina and establishing its own order, and they were seeking protection from the regular army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you watched the meeting between Arkan and Biljana Plavsic, and you explained the footage we were shown here, Plavsic kissing Arkan. And from point 11 or paragraph 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness got a copy of his statement? Yes. Mr. Omeragic, if you want to follow, you can, if you're referred to particular paragraphs. Paragraph 11, apparently. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And in that paragraph, you say Arkan showed respect towards her when they kissed, and she said to him, "My child." Well, she's much older than him, so that wouldn't be anything unusual. Is that right, Mr. Omeragic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that Plavsic said that Arkan had saved Bijeljina from the crimes which the Muslims prepared and intended to execute because before that they had blocked Bijeljina. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what she said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did she say that for whatever reason or because it was correct? She came there together with Abdic.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was being prepared, but the preparations didn't last long, because the next day after the first shots -- after the first clashes, Arkan entered Bijeljina and started taking control. He started bringing in his men and his order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what you say in point 12 of your statement, "Plavsic said on that occasion that they had saved the people from a crime, from the crimes."

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean, "Save the people from the crimes." Let the victims speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Mr. Omeragic. You are testifying on the basis of your statement and not on the basis of the examination-in-chief. So I don't know one way or another, and that's why I'm asking you with reference to what it says in your statement, to clarify that particular point, because this is what you say. And it is point 12, or if you haven't got it, it's on page 3 of the statement, the one but last paragraph. You say: "She stated that Arkan had saved Bijeljina from the crimes that the Muslims had prepared and were to conduct against them. She stated that he had saved the people from the crimes which the Muslims were preparing against the Serbs. Fikret Abdic did not react or respond." That is your statement.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means -- well, tell me if I've interrupted you. What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the whole point. Mrs. Plavsic said that Arkan had saved the people from the crimes which the Muslims were preparing against the Serbs. At the same time, we had 41 victims proclaimed over the radio, so within those victims, 38 or 39 of them were non-Serbs, of the total number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have those facts and figures, but let's just focus on this for a moment. She said what she said because she thought that it was true, and now you add that Fikret Abdic did not respond, on the basis of which one could conclude that he too considered that to be correct, what you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't make any such conclusion, and the witness can't answer why Fikret Abdic did not respond, but go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just taking note of what it says here, Mr. May. And that is what the witness stated, or at least that's what it says in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it true that to a journalist of the newspaper Politika Biljana Plavsic said that Arkan had done what he should have done and that he brought peace to Bijeljina? That's what it says in point 27, that he prevented crimes from being committed, ill-deeds.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And Fikret Abdic, the leader of the Muslims, that is to say, and as you know, a man who won the greatest number of votes on the list in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the election there, and on the basis of that he should have been president of the Presidency, didn't question that at all. Was that how it was or not?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fikret Abdic didn't question many things. It was -- he was quite an individual, character. When he should have responded, he didn't respond. And when he was supposed to say anything that would take more courage, be more courageous or frank, he didn't make the effort to utter any such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Omeragic. I don't suppose you want to say that Fikret Abdic could have had anything in his attitude to things which would be contrary to Muslim interests?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite certain that Mr. Abdic was ready, was prepared -- was unprepared to do anything against Muslim interests. I think it's a long story there, and I think it would take us to a dead end and an unnecessary discussion along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the Presidency in the name of the Muslims, and as you will recall, there were two declared Muslims, two Croats, two Serbs, and one Yugoslav in the Presidency. Those two Muslims were Izetbegovic and Abdic, or Abdic and Izetbegovic, because Abdic won more votes than Izetbegovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, you wrote in your statement, in point 15: "At one stage of the visit I approached one of the Territorial Defence members and he did not know who I was, so I asked him, `Did you cut down those balijas?' He thought that I was one of his men and he said words to the effect, `Yes, we have killed quite a lot of them.'" That's what you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that really happen?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you have the list of victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about the list of victims. Perhaps I didn't read your article carefully enough. Where do you actually say that in your article? Could you point out the passage, because I don't seem to be able to find it myself.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: It's in between the text, the grey portion. You mean the victims, where it says "victims," that paragraph titled "The victims," after the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure we're talking about the same thing. I'm asking you to find this event in the text where you say, "Did you cut down those balijas?" and he gave you the answer he gave you, or you're asking him as a sort of provocation, in fact, because you're a Muslim. So you're asking this Serb, "Did you cut down those balijas?" And his answer was, "Yes," along those lines. As you say, "words to that effect." I wasn't able to find that in your article.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it exist in your article?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No, not in the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how come such a major point which you state in your statement you did not include into the text that you titled "The Bloody Bajram in Bijeljina" and all the rest of it? How come such a cardinal point was left out, when you asked someone, "Did you cut down those balijas," and he said, "Yes, we killed quite a lot of them"? How come you didn't put that in the article yet you put it in your statement in the year 2001? Did you invent that event, Mr. Omeragic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for you to finish, to complete what you're saying. I did not put into my text, into my article, even a tenth of what went on, of all the events that occurred in Bijeljina, because a newspaper article is always short, too short to include everything, to publish everything, but I could tell you endless tales, go on for days telling you about what I experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As concerns the quantitative, if I can say that, the quantitative approach, your statement is roughly the length of your newspaper article. I haven't counted the words, of course, but I don't suppose the article has more worth than the statement. So how come such a cardinal fact that you mention in your statement when you ask a soldier, "Did you cut down those balijas," and he says, "Yes, many," how come you didn't include that in your article?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I think that the statement is at least four times as long as my newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you considered this not to be essential, and that's why you didn't include it into your article, this conversation.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, because there are no names or proof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, then, please: You say that there was a journalist whose name was Golubovic, a journalist from TV Sarajevo, Velibor Golubovic, and they were rough towards him and shoved him downstairs. Is it true that Golubovic was the son-in-law of General Kukanjac, the commander of the army district?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Golubovic, a journalist for RTV Sarajevo, was Kukanjac's son-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were rough towards him?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan's man was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were -- they handled this man in a rough way, and he was somebody who was close to a general of the JNA; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I can explain everything to you and can tell you that at the moment when this colleague, Mr. Golubovic, said that he was a Television Sarajevo journalist, that Arkan told two of his men, his escorts in black uniform -- he was in black uniform and he said to his escorts in the territorial green uniform, he said, "Take him away." And at that point this man says, "Well, you're surely not going to kill me," or, "Please don't kill me," something like that, and as you can see, he had some assumptions too. And at the time Mrs. Biljana Plavsic's driver rushed up and whispered something to Arkan's man, whispered in his ear, and I heard him mention the name Kukanjac, but that wasn't enough for this man, and Arkan's man also said worse things. He said, "Take him away."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from what you're telling us, they seem to have been in some kind of conflict with the army.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that's already been confirmed. That was confirmed in the requests and entreaties to Arkan that the town should be left to the JNA when he rejected this emphatically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the army tried not to enter into this conflict but to control the town and protect the population; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody asked the JNA anything, but Arkan was in command there and had the final say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what grounds are you able to say that the general - I forget which general, whether it was Jankovic or Prascevic - that he was reporting to Arkan. Did you ever hear him reporting to Arkan? Did you hear him reporting to Arkan in any way?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I saw him going up to him. He took four steps forward -- you can see that on the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I saw on the footage was that a man in uniform was saluting somebody else in uniform, which means saluting by bringing up his hand to his cap. That is how they would salute each other on the street, one army man to another. I have seen that many times, both as a pupil, a student, and as a general citizen at large. When somebody meets somebody else, they greet them in this way. It's not reporting of any kind, it's just a greeting. Did you hear him actually report to him?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He stood to attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where can you see on the footage that he stood to attention?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it on the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he stood to attention in front of Arkan, this general, General Prascevic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do, report to him?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: He greeted him, reported to him, and I don't think you can see Arkan on the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: On the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No you can only see Arkan afterwards, when they shake hands.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Arkan is standing there leisurely and calmly and only once General Prascevic had saluted, had greeted him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can't see that on the footage.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't have, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if they greeted one another, does that mean that the general reported to him?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: That's what it looked like to me. It looked like him reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. It looked like it to you, but did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, so did I. So when you're reporting to someone, you have to say something, you have to report something to the person you're reporting to, whereas here they just greeted -- met each other and greeted each other.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's how it was. I stand by what I said. Arkan was standing leisurely and calmly and waiting, and if you look at the footage carefully, you will see Prascevic taking four steps forward, standing to attention, reporting, and then carrying on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but Prascevic is approaching that spot where they were standing. So he would have necessarily to take some steps forward?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've exhausted this topic. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have too. Yes, I agree. We have exhausted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell me, please -- I have to collect my thoughts and remember. You mentioned a man called Predrag and describe how the two of us, Arkan's -- how Arkan's soldiers took you by the arm and wanted to take you somewhere, take you away. This is in point 20. And a man called Predrag prevented this, and there was some kind of argument that took place. That's in point 20. So they didn't arrest you, actually, did they?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: You were not arrested, were you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I was not arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they had intended to do that and then they gave it up?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: They showed that when they took me under the arm and tried to take me away, though I was told that I was some sort of an escort of Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, nobody touched you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: It was just then that they wanted to take me away, but this young man saved me. And this man in black uniform, an Arkan man, said he was going to kill me, and they -- and then he said, "Don't let me kill him here in front of you." And then he put this short barrel -- rather, long-barrelled pistol, I can't remember that too well, actually. I think it was handmade. He put this barrel on my head, to my temple. I could feel it. He was threatening, and he was quarrelling with this other man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: The door was opened, because we were making a lot of noise. Arkan wouldn't let me go into the meeting. And the door opened, and Arkan appeared. I can tell you, he just raised his finger like this and pointed it over there in a different direction, and as the door was opened, everyone was standing. These two men in green uniform who were listening to Arkan took me by the arm, and Arkan indicated with his finger that they should go. And they ran down the steps. Anyway they disappeared. Then Arkan when he opened the door said, "What's all this noise?" They were all standing there, and then he just moved his finger and these two disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. You were not arrested. An incident occurred, but nothing happened to you.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Thank God, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned in this short -- now, I don't know whether it was in the summary or you actually said so, that you saw men wearing old JNA uniforms, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these men in old JNA uniforms were not members of the JNA, were they? They were local TO members.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether it is true that in Bijeljina, at the time, Abdic made a speech? You were following that whole visit. Did he speak on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present where Mr. Abdic spoke. It was at that meeting which lasted about 35 minutes, not more than that, and I had no access there because Arkan turned me back. When I was about to go in, he was standing at the door deciding who would go and who wouldn't, and he wouldn't let me go in only, as well as this Golubovic with his crew. I think that one of the cameramen entered without a camera, but he wouldn't let Golubovic in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My interest is not for Golubovic right now. In paragraph 24, you say that, "I was told that Abdic's speech was broadcast and that it lasted five to six minutes. That is what I heard, but I didn't hear it broadcast." Was Abdic's speech broadcast by the radio?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, it was not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us make sure we understand one another. From paragraph 24, I gathered that you were claiming that they didn't broadcast the telephone conversations which Abdic had with people who were calling him directly on an open phone in the studio and that was not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I heard from one of the young men, guards, who were in uniform. I took a transistor radio, I saw it when we were entering, and I put it next to Mr. Abdic's driver. And I was looking for the music on the radio that could be heard from the studio so as to hear what Mr. Abdic was saying and talking to people who were calling in, and I was looking for that music but I didn't hear anything. I didn't hear Mr. Abdic speaking with the people at the other end of the line. This was not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the very fact that listeners were informed that Abdic is in the studio, doesn't that confirm that he was speaking? It's another matter whether they were broadcasting live his conversations with citizens on the telephone, but surely the citizens must have heard him speaking to be able to call up and ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: They need not necessarily be in the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would they know? How would they call him up if they didn't know that he was on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: He was just there. The public didn't hear him. These complaints or requests or disputes could not be heard on the radio, which means it simply wasn't broadcast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that Abdic did not speak in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Not in public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nothing of what Abdic said in Bijeljina was broadcast. Is that what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a the transistor radio and didn't hear anything. While I was listening, and I think I was listening for about half a hour, I didn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were told that he spoke for about five or six minutes on the radio and that this was broadcast. They told you that. This is something you also heard?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: He didn't speak at all over the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say, "I was told that Abdic's speech was broadcast and that it lasted five to six minutes." I'm reading the whole sentence for you. "I was told that Abdic's speech was broadcast and that it lasted about six minutes."

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: That is what I was told, but I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what it says in your statement. It's true that you say that you didn't hear it, but you also say that you were told that it was broadcast and that it lasted five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Someone may have told me that. I listened for about 25 minutes or half an hour. I saw Mr. Abdic in the studio. I was across the way from him. He -- glass separated us, and I could hear him and see him speaking on the phone with citizens calling him up, but at the same time, I heard the music which should have been the backdrop to his conversations there in the breaks until a line is established. I just heard the music. I didn't hear Mr. Abdic's voice. So I wasn't sure whether he was given any time to speak or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were with Abdic all the time, it would appear that he didn't see what you claim you saw. What did he say as his position, his observation or his condemnation of something that had happened if things happened in the way you portray them?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing. Mr. Abdic even had a kind of argument with me on the way back. I asked Mr. Abdic, "What are you going to say?" He just waved his hand and there was an argument. In the short time I was with Mr. Abdic, I realised only one thing, and that is that either that he sought to be quite impersonal or that was part of his nature, his character, not to react even when it was necessary or when it was unnecessary. He was just a man walking around seeking peace, saying that he was a peace advocate, at the same time saying nothing for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt you. You've got three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I haven't managed to develop your habit to keep watching the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Omeragic, why in your statement you don't mention this passive attitude by Abdic which is very strange. He is a member of the Presidency. He came there and he's not reacting to something that happened there, according to what you claim. Why did you not write anything about such a position which was absolutely specific if it was the way you put it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Let us say that I considered this to be his strategy that I didn't want to interfere with, allegedly seeking peace with Mrs. Plavsic. This time I went with them because I couldn't pass otherwise, but on other occasions I went to Bosanski Brod, Derventa and other places where they tried, only tried, to talk about peace and to act as some sort of mediators. So I believed that this was part of his strategy that I didn't want to interfere with as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the meeting in the JNA barracks in Tuzla where Plavsic said, once again, that Arkan had saved Bijeljina of the crime -- of a crime against the Serbs and that you responded roughly by saying, "How could you say something like that when you saw what the situation was like over there?" Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did react.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw the hospitals, you saw the Muslims who had fled and sought shelter in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Plavsic said, "No. More Serbs were killed." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what eventually did you conclude? Is it what you wrote here in the frame in your article? And how did you find that out, what you wrote here? You are saying that you informed them in Tuzla that a crime had been committed against the Muslims in Bijeljina. Now, tell me, did you explain to them how you learnt about that for them to believe you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand the question. Who had to believe me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you spoke out at this meeting in Tuzla, that there had been crimes against the Muslims in Bijeljina, when Plavsic retorted, "No, there were more Serbs killed." Did you inform them about what you had learnt?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't inform Mrs. Plavsic about anything, or Mr. Abdic, because I am not in such a position as to be able to do that. I was a man looking at things with my own eyes and coming to my own conclusions. Later on, these proved to be correct when the later report of Vlado Mrkic brought over a list of victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But my question a moment ago about the meeting with the JNA in Tuzla and about what Plavsic said and what you said, how you responded, this whole story in paragraph 29 of your statement, you didn't report any of that in your article.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: It is true that I didn't write anything about that in that article, but I'm telling you again not ten articles would have been sufficient to cover everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, if it is my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you went to Bosanski Brod, that it was held by the HVO and that the town had already been destroyed. You say that in paragraph 32. Who destroyed Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, according to what I know, in Lijeska, in the north-eastern part of Bosanski Brod municipality, a territory had been formed with ethnically pure Serb inhabitants. It was known as the Serb Brod. And as far as I know, the main person there was Mile Radovanovic, who used to be a taxi driver in Brod.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the one but last paragraph of your statement you say, "Some two, three, or four days after that, Abdic and Franjo Boras --" Franjo Boras is a Croat, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "-- visited Bosanski Brod. I visited at the same time. It was possible for me to get there alone. Boras and Abdic entered the municipality building together, and the town was under HVO control. The town was already destroyed and damaged." Which means you arrived in Bosanski Brod, it was under the control of the Croatian forces, and it was already destroyed and damaged. Who destroyed and damaged Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: While I was there, there was from Lijeska, from the Serb part, and these probably retaliated, as far as I was able to see, so they fired their artillery shells in that direction too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do have questions of the witness. Questioned by Mr. Kay:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how many times did Arkan and Biljana Plavsic kiss on this occasion in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I think three times as far as I was able to see on the clip and as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at your article which has been exhibited in the trial, Exhibit 564. I'm just going to go through the stages of the article. You describe in general terms at the beginning about the visit to Bijeljina and your impression of it. You described Fikret Abdic going to the barracks and then the summons to municipality hall where Mrs. Plavsic is waiting and you're about to meet with Arkan. You describe Abdic going to municipality hall, and then after the meeting you describe going around houses to speak to people with Arkan being there. I'm on page 3 now, and you describe the hospital. And on page 4 in the English, you describe then going to Radio Bijeljina where Fikret Abdic is to talk to the Muslim listeners. And then on the last page, you describe Biljana Plavsic, General Prascevic, General Jankovic, and Arkan in the park. You describe Plavsic being interviewed by Ekspres Politika, and she kisses Arkan good-bye. What kiss have we been watching in this courtroom, a kiss of greeting and approval or a kiss good-bye to Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: We saw the kiss upon arrival, upon their first meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this article you mention nothing about a kiss on arrival. The only kiss you mention is a kiss good-bye?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a kiss on arrival?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention it in your article?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I think it's just due to forgetfulness, but I was there. You could see that on the footage. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you describe in your article is an army where a corporal had more authority than two broken-down generals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, isn't this just a matter of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's going to be what the situation is in Bijeljina rather than a matter of argument. The article plainly deals with the situation where people are sheltering at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's the point of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the barracks, you described people sheltering in the JNA barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you describe is a situation in Bijeljina where Arkan had control of that town.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he being asked to leave that town?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: More precisely put, to leave the town to the JNA, to hand it over to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was being told to go.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you saw, he had with him forces who were in support of him, and he had control of that town.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that moment in Bijeljina, power was with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If I may just ask the witness a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Agha:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've just established that according to you, Arkan was in fact in control of that town, and you had gone along there to see what had been happening in Bijeljina, and you witnessed the very senior general who you mentioned, Prascevic of the 2nd Military District. Now, when he came to Bijeljina, did he come with tanks and artillery in order to expel Arkan who had attacked the town?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No. They arrived in ordinary cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In actual fact, what you witnessed was the deputy general of the 2nd Military District of the People's Army salute and greet the man who had just attacked Bijeljina and other Yugoslav citizens; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's really for the witness to say what he witnessed rather than for the advocate to tell him what he witnessed, which I think is what was happening here.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to apologise to him or anybody. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you kindly answer the question, please, witness, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could rephrase it. Rephrase it, please, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, rather than fighting off Arkan, how did the general of the 2nd Military District approach him when he met him in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as can be seen from that clip, General Prascevic came almost like some sort of a neutral negotiator, as some sort of accidental figure in a town which was absolutely ruled by Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he left?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They went back in the third car, the one you could see us coming in. They went back together to Sarajevo, General Prascevic, Fikret Abdic and Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question is that the accused and my learned friend has placed quite a lot of emphasis on what you did and what you did not say in your statement before the investigators as opposed to what you said in your newspaper article. And the suggestion was that perhaps many things had been left out of your statement which you had mentioned in your article which were important and as to why they weren't mentioned. But if I may draw your attention to your actual article, I think that there are many important matters mentioned in your article, such as massacres of the population, the cleaning out of this place by Arkan,, which are also not in your statement which can be regarded as very important. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's quite correct to say that because you witnessed so many things of significance they couldn't possibly all be mentioned in a short newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, if ever there was a leading question, it was that one. You suggest the answer to the witness. He just says yes. Let him answer. Yes, Mr. Omeragic, you should have the last word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I'm talking about these things, everything I was saying in answer to Mr. Milosevic and you, at one point when I returned from Bijeljina, I was in a desperate situation because of everything I had seen but also because I feared that whatever I had seen in Bijeljina would be mirrored in other places of Bosnia and Herzegovina in even worse form. And at the time, I was so lost that even things that appeared to you to be of key significance were omitted, and the kiss of death that is repeatedly referred to between Mrs. Plavsic and Arkan, I didn't mention that, you see, and now it is in the focus of attention. So I returned from Bijeljina as a man who I must say was met with shells, because the first shells started falling in Sarajevo that day. And when I was about to write the text on the 6th, the first shells had already fallen and the first casualties. So this kind of distractedness contributed to my leaving out some important things regarding my visit to Bijeljina from my article because of this all coinciding and because the tragedy started of which I was a part for three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Pack, I understand that you would wish to try and get through this witness today. Obviously that will be desirable. We can sit on until 2.00 or thereabouts, but since the accused must have his hour, the only way I should think it's going to be done is for you to forego your time at the beginning. You may want to consider that in the interests of trying to finish the witness. We can read the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I won't read the summary out in that case. If I may, I will ask that the first two -- the two statements for this Witness B-1453, and the exhibits are tabs 3, 4, and 5 be admitted into evidence pursuant to 89(F). I will ask the witness to deal with them, but I ask that because they were the subject of a 92 bis (B) application that was granted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the formalities haven't been concluded under 92 bis. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're asking us merely to deal with it now under 89(F). The witness must, of course, go through the necessary procedure to clarify, ratify, authenticate the document and declare it's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll ask him to do that. Examined by Ms. Pack:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could the witness please be handed tab 2, please, his statement at tab 2 of the bundle. And that's the English version. The front page of the English version, please, the cover page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, look at the cover page, please. Your details are identified -- your name is identified on the cover page of that statement? Just your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see your signature at the bottom of at that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And go through to the end of that statement and look, please, at your signature at the end of that statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you initialled the bottom of each page of that English-language statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's dated the 23rd of January, 1997. Witness, have you since read a B/C/S version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, subject to two corrections which we'll come to, are the contents of that statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, it is truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the B/C/S version of that statement. It just follows on from the English at the same tab, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd ask you to look at the cover page. Is there something you want to correct there on the cover page, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Have I to correct the word "Bosniak." I'm a Bosnian. I was born in Bosnia, so I'm a Bosnian, not a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please turn to paragraph 19. Witness, is there anything in that paragraph you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: In this paragraph, I would like to correct the surname Milicic. The commander's surname was Milincic, with an "N". Because there's another man who was called Milicic who was there. This is with an "N."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown tab 1 of the bundle, the cover page of the English version of his witness statement dated 18th of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, again please look at the cover page. Can you see your signature on that page at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I see it. It is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your signature on the next three pages of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, please, at the next document, which is the B/C/S version of the statement. Witness, have you had a chance, since being in The Hague, to read the B/C/S version of your statement dated the 18th of April, 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I have had an opportunity of reading it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are the contents of that statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: It is true and correct. I gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you made that statement, did you pass over to investigator from the OTP three documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, I did give those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Those documents, Your Honour, appear at paragraphs -- sorry, at tabs 3, 4, and 5. I would ask then that those two statements and those three tabbed exhibit tabs be admitted into evidence pursuant to 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 565, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, turn, please, to tab 6 of the binder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown tab 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look -- look, please, at that document. Can you tell us, please - it is dated the 7th of May, 1992 - who it is from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: This document is from the chief of the Bijeljina public security station, Predrag Jesuric, addressed to the minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to the establishment of the police and carrying out assignments in Brcko, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I do recognise the signature of Jesuric, because he was my superior directly. I know him personally, and I recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, please, at the third paragraph of that document, starting, "Pursuant to the decision ..."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, if that -- what that -- what that paragraph describes and if what that paragraph describes is familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: It describes the fact that police units were set up to go to Brcko to look after the property, both public and private property, and I was among the units sent to Brcko. But we weren't able to carry out our assignment because we were prevented from doing so by others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are the others you were prevented from doing your task by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: We were prevented by the ones from the Territorial Defence, the Chetniks, so-called Chetniks, who looted en masse. We didn't enter into a conflict with them, we just stood by and watched and saw what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Those matters, Your Honour, are dealt with in the first statement at paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Couple of points of clarification. If you could just go to tab 1, please, of the binder and look at the B/C/S version of your witness statement, paragraph 7. Witness, you describe in paragraph 7 having seen convoys coming from Serbia carrying military equipment. Tell us, please, when you saw those convoys.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I saw those convoys in April and May, and I personally accompanied them with our official vehicles from Serbia to Majevica, Zvornik, and their destinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's April and May, 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes. 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see these convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I saw the convoys that I accompanied. I accompanied them ten times during those two months, at least ten times. I saw them go across the bridge, rail bridge across the Sava River. I was there at a checkpoint, and I would see daily between two or three convoys, trains, actually, transporting these goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the trains, I'm asking you about the convoys. How many times did you escort convoys from Serbia, coming from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I personally escorted those convoys at least ten times, the ones coming from Serbia across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many trucks or vehicles made up those convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Usually they would be made up of between 10 to 20 vehicles, I would say. I didn't count, but I would judge it to be at that figure. They were heavy-duty trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, please, the locations where those convoys were going.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: When I escorted them, I would escort them sometimes towards Majevica up there, a village by Triboj [phoen], that is where the line ends. That's where the battlefield was. So I went that far and when I went to Brcko, I would go as far as Brezovo Polje which is the final point after which you come to the battlefield and then to Zvornik up to Sepak on the bridge at Sepak. I accompanied them there and then us police would return and they were deployed elsewhere. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was all in the course of your duties as a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You describe in paragraph 7 seeing trains carrying military equipment. Please tell us when you saw those trains, which months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I saw all that also in April and May because I worked at the checkpoint at Sremska Raca and there is a railway line coming from Serbia passing that way and they were transporting tanks by trains. I saw the tanks and I saw the heavy weapons to Bijeljina, because the railway line ends there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trains did you see pass, how often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: When I worked, I would work for at least 12 hours in one go, so during my shifts, two to three convoys carrying equipment of this kind, two to three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, I think your time is up if we're to finish this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1453, is it true that in Bijeljina some barricades had been erected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: It is correct that the barricades were erected. Ordinary, actually, checkpoints, roadblocks. They would put a tree trunk or a vehicle or something to block the road in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, in town. Now, is it true that that was organised by the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: That was organised by the people for them to be able to have an overview of who was coming into town and leaving town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say organised by the people, and I said the Party of Democratic Action, was it in fact organised by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Muslims organised it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the roadblocks were organised in Bijeljina by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: The Muslims lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that at the head of the Party of Democratic Action was Seval Begic at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Seval Begic, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct that next to him occupying a high post, one of the organisers of those roadblocks, was Alija Saracevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Alija Saracevic did occupy a post, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslims blocked the entire centre of town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I can't say that the whole centre of town was blocked off. They put up roadblocks in individual parts of town to exercise control, as I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember that at that time the Muslims took weapons out of mosques and that they took control of the town in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No. Nobody had any weapons, nor did they take weapons out of mosques, especially not out of mosques. Well, they couldn't have taken control of the town when it was Arkan's men who had control of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about before that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No, nobody occupied town because it was Arkan who occupied it. These were just roadblocks for control purposes and supervision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the town was blocked but not taken control of. That's your explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember the snipers' nests in the water tower, Zitopromet, the silos, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: There were no Snipers' nests anywhere. Arkan's men just invented that so that they could feel free to shoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how come Stojan Stojanovic was wounded by these snipers who had opened fire? I'm sure you will remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know about Stojan Stojanovic or that he was wounded. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that this operation undertaken by the operations in Bijeljina was premature, judging by their plan or rather with respect to the plan devised by the Party of Democratic Action to start on the first day of the Bajram holiday, the 4th and 5th of April, most probably, to launch the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I was never a member of any party so I don't know about this. Nobody informed me. I was in the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these roadblocks and the barricade at Bijeljina set up by the Muslims, this upset the plans, premature plans?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. The roadblocks were set up because somebody threw a bomb, a hand-grenade into a coffee bar and some ten people were injured. So this was a reaction to that and that's why the roadblocks and barricades were set up, not for any other kind of operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that at the time the Muslim leadership considered and Izetbegovic considered that by simultaneous drives throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina could they be assured of success?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know about that, I wasn't a member of the SDA party. I just did police work, policing, nothing else, so I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now when we're speaking about the roadblocks and the blockades of Bijeljina, is it true that the Muslims at that time in the centre of town erected these barricades and held the hospital, the municipality building, the electrical supplies building, they had control of all that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No. The barricades were not in the centre of town. They were in the suburbs when you come in from the villages so they could control who was coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Municipal Assembly building which was also taken -- and also the electrical -- electricity board building that was taken over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I was personally in the electricity board building there providing security. Nobody overtook that building or the Municipal Assembly building. The roadblocks and barricades why just out on the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know on that same night the 31st of March, a warehouse was looted at the barracks and that weapons were handed out publicly to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: The barracks and warehouse was in Pecine, not in town. So there wasn't a barracks or a warehouse of the barracks there nor was -- were weapons publicly distributed to people in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the park? Was a bunker erected there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: There was never a bunker in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that blockade at Bijeljina which you describe yourself and say that this was done by the Muslims, erected by the Muslims, that that caused and triggered off the conflict in Bijeljina, not by an attack of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No. This wasn't a barricade. It was just an ordinary roadblock. They were ordinary roadblocks such as checkpoints to control the comings and goings to see that people weren't bringing in weapons. They weren't blockades in the proper sense of the word at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Because you say there was nothing at the silo, firearms were found at the silo and I assume you ought to know that. You were a policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. No weapons were found there. They just collected up the hunting rifles that had been registered with licenses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 31st of March did a number of Albanians arrive in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No. All the Albanians were killed in Bijeljina who were there, the locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I never saw that in any piece of information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: There's a photograph about four Albanians being killed in front of a butcher's shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it true that the Muslims expected help from Tuzla which never arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were expecting any assistance, but they couldn't have expected it if you know Bijeljina. Bijeljina was surrounded by Serb villages on all sides, 20 to 30 kilometres in depth. They're all Serbian villages all around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It was surrounded by Serb villages you say, and it was blocked by the Muslims, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Only the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The town of Bijeljina itself. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: There were just roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on that same day, the 4th of April, did anybody call the JNA into Bijeljina and declare a general mobilisation on that same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Who called whom? Who called for a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: On the 4th of April everything was over in Bijeljina. It was quiet on the 4th of April because it was Bajram. It was a calm day, nothing special was going on. Everything was over by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about the identification of the people killed when everything was over, anything was finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: It was publicly proclaimed that 41 persons were killed in the conflicts and there is a list published by Radio Bijeljina and there was a list published in the papers, the list of those people killed. And these were all ordinary civilians, two children I think were killed, two women, an invalid, and many other citizens, young men, all civilians. None of them were in uniforms, nor was there a war on of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the exact number of casualties in Bijeljina during those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: All I know is the -- what was published via broadcast via Radio Bijeljina and that was 41 and there was a list that appeared in the Semberija newspaper, as it was called. Now, how many people were actually killed, I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you only know what was published in those local newspapers, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how many of them were Serbs? How many were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Of the 41 killed, there was one Serb, a man called Mica. He was a little simple and -- just happened to be there. And then there was another man called Milo Kurjak, Veljko Lukic, Kurjak's brother, and there was a Croatian lady, I think her name was Milka Lazarevic. That's as far as I, know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. We had different names put forward here. I'm not asking you to remember all the names of all the victims at the time. But do you know that in another settlement called Gvozderic, Muslims clashed amongst themselves and that there were casualties there too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I know the Gvozdevic settlement, and there was no clash among the Muslims themselves in Bijeljina and there were no casualties either, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that during the process of calming down the situation in town the Muslims brought in over 500 long-barrels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No, they didn't have those weapons. The Muslims didn't have any weapons. They just had the hunting rifles. If you call those long-barrels, then that is possible. There were quite a few hunters in the area, so they had carbines and hunting weapons that they had licenses to carry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you as a policeman should have known the number of long-barrels there were, that over 500 rifles were handed over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the two incidents that you talk about which came prior to the erection of the roadblocks, were there in fact attacks on two cafes called the Istanbul and the Srbija cafe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: There was a bomb, a hand-grenade thrown into the Istanbul cafe, and the next night there was a clash between young people in the Istanbul cafe and the Srbija cafe. That was the other night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that with these incidents both in the Srbija cafe and in the other cafe, the Istanbul cafe, and generally speaking what was going on, that nobody had anything to do with that incident outside Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean outside Bijeljina. I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody who was not from Bijeljina that took part in those incidents in those two cafes, the Srbija and Istanbul cafes, taking part there and everything that came prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: I don't think that it was anybody outside Bijeljina when those incidents took place. I knew this young man who threw the hand-grenade at the Istanbul cafe and that I know the next night there was another incident between the Srbija and Istanbul cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This young man from Borovo he was arrested straight away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: He was taken to the police station. Now, what actually happened to him after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, as you talk about Mirko Blagojevic as one of the organisers of the conflicts in Bijeljina. Is he a man from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, he is a native of Bijeljina, born there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you describe him as wearing a black fur cap. He wasn't a wearing a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: No. He was a representative of the Radical Party and of the so-called Chetniks. He publicly declared himself to be a Chetnik and wore such a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up, and I apologise to the interpreters because of the time constraints. I'm trying to fit in with them. You say that he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party, but that's in Bijeljina, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1453
utterances.text: Yes, he was president of that party.
